https://www.politico.eu/article/gabriel-.text: PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is trying to jump-start his presidential prospects by taking advantage of his rivals enjoying France’s cherished August break. Attal, a former prime minister who now leads President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist political party Renaissance, is betting that by keeping a busy schedule during the holiday and meeting with people across the country — including those at vineyards, markets and ports as well as vacationers in picturesque seaside towns — he can show voters what sets him apart from the field. “It’s a rather bourgeois assumption to think that all French people take time off or go on vacation,” said a representative for Attal’s team who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about campaign dynamics. “There’s no way he’s going to suspend his campaign over the summer.” Advertisement But political reality is also forcing Attal to campaign in August for the vote in April of next year. If he wants a real shot at catching up in the polls, there’s little time to waste. Surveys have consistently shown the 37-year-old trailing Edouard Philippe, his main ideological rival for centrist and center-right votes. Given the contest goes to a two-candidate runoff if nobody wins a majority in the first round, the two men have tentatively agreed that only one of them should be on the ballot so they don’t split their shared voter base — which could cost both of them a spot in the second round. Philippe, far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau are all among the presidential hopefuls taking long summer breaks, only interrupting their time off for the occasional op-ed or statement on major events like the wildfires that ravaged southwest France. Edouard Philippe speaks at a rally in northern Paris on July 5, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images Their reasoning for slowing down during the peak holiday season is straightforward: Voters want to rest and recharge, so candidates shouldn’t harass them with politics and should instead enjoy one last bit of respite before the race enters its decisive stretch. “We shouldn’t bother the French people while they’re on vacation,” said a Retailleau adviser. Attal is betting otherwise that a summer spent campaigning can help close the gap in the polls. “A campaign is about winning over the French one by one … [Attal] wants to show that he’s more determined than the others,” added his adviser. The right track It’s unclear for now to what extent Attal’s summer work will reap dividends with voters, as most pollsters who would investigate that question have themselves set out-of-office messages. But the absence of other candidates on the campaign trail has given Attal an opportunity to dominate headlines, and he’s used it to make a play for right-wing voters. Advertisement At the start of the month, Attal, a member of parliament who represents a Paris suburb, gave an interview to the right-wing weekly Le Journal du Dimanche in which he called for lower immigration, a sweeping streamlining of France’s administrative procedures and more effective enforcement of criminal sentences. He then traveled to western France, where, in front of cameras, he confronted a group of French gens du voyage — a legal classification for traditionally itinerant communities, including Roma and Manouche, and long a target of the French right — who had occupied land without authorization. The encounter can be seen below in a report from CNEWS, in French. French municipalities are required to provide designated stopping sites for traveling communities, but those obligations are not always met — or the sites provided are insufficient — sometimes resulting in unauthorized occupations of public or private land. For both Attal and Philippe, making inroads on the right will be crucial. Macron’s 2022 reelection was buoyed by older, more affluent voters who had traditionally backed conservatives. But Philippe begins that contest with a built-in advantage. Advertisement He is a former member of the conservative party Les Républicains and has always identified as a man of the right. Attal, who started his political career in the youth wing of the center-left Socialists, has resisted the label. One conservative minister in the current French government, who has not endorsed a candidate for 2027, readily described Philippe as belonging to his political camp. Attal, the minister said, has a “very flexible” ideological spine. Sarah Paillou and Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

Henning Kaiser - DPA Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save BERLIN (AP) — Authorities said Wednesday that two incidents that disrupted power distribution systems in eastern and western Germany were being investigated as possible acts of sabotage, with one also being examined for possible links to terrorism. Multiple explosive devices were found Tuesday morning at a substation near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg in northeastern Germany. Hours later, a short circuit knocked power lines out of service at the Bergheim power substation near Cologne in western Germany — an incident described by security officials as a deliberate act. Neither incident affected the general power supply in their areas. Authorities are investigating the incidents but have not named any suspects, nor have they said if they could be connected. They say possible suspects could include a foreign power or left-wing extremists. The developments come as Germany is on high alert after the government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 using a drone laden with explosives. “A substation is the nerve center of our daily lives. Anyone who attacks it isn’t just attacking a tin roof — they’re attacking our country, our economy, our daily lives, and all of us,” said Herbert Reul, the interior minister of North Rhine-Westphalia state, where Bergheim is located. “Critical infrastructure is the Achilles’ heel of our society. Perhaps we haven’t taken this issue seriously enough over the years.” Authorities suspect ‘terrorism’ in the incident in eastern Germany Brandenburg police said Wednesday on X that they had launched an investigation into the suspected formation of a terrorist organization “in conjunction with causing an explosion involving explosives and the destruction of important work equipment.” “What we are currently experiencing is a hybrid threat and we therefore cannot rule out the possibility that foreign powers are behind it,” Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann told public broadcaster ARD. Emergency responders searched the area for evidence, prompting road closures, authorities said Wednesday. Large groups of investigators combed through the area for clues. Officials described the explosives as “rocketlike objects equipped with a propellant charge” similar to fireworks. They said there were more than a dozen, but that only one managed to carry a cable into the high-voltage power line to establish a conductive connection to the ground, the German news agency dpa reported. Short circuit in western Germany was caused deliberately, officials say Bright flashes of light could be seen along several power lines at the Bergheim power substation near Cologne in western Germany on Tuesday evening, said Reul. “It wasn’t a broken switch, it was intentional. It was a criminal act,” Reul said. “We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign government and left-wing extremism. We cannot rule out either possibility at this time.” RWE, the company that operates the power substation, said five coal-fired power plant units with a combined capacity of 4,200 megawatts were taken offline after the incident. Police said investigators found six launch devices in a nearby cornfield. Chief Detective Michael Esser told reporters that the devices were supposedly designed to use pyrotechnic devices to lift a wire high above the power lines. The investigation has so far found that “the perpetrators deliberately caused a short circuit by placing conductive material — presumably cables — over the overhead line.” Security officials from both regions were in contact and closely checking for possible connections between the Brandenburg and Bergheim incidents, Reul said. Two power plant units were running again by Wednesday afternoon; another one was expected to go back online later on Wednesday. Work is underway to bring the two remaining units back online by the weekend. German power infrastructure has previously been affected under similar circumstances. Suspected left-wing extremists set fire to high-voltage lines near a power plant in southwest Berlin in January. Ciobanu reported from Warsaw. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-expected-to.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NLAS Aftermath of a drone attack near the Ukrainian-Moldovan border Image: OdeskaODA/Telegram Advertisement Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare. The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common. For the Baltic states, Poland , Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately. Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Drones violate Moldovan and Romanian airspace This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily. Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta. The wreckage of a drone found in Moldova Image: Polizei der Republik Moldau The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine. In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska , 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine. On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military. Polish Prime Minister Tusk says Europe needs to prepare Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them. Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate. Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine. Donald Tusk has warned that Poland has to prepare for possible drone attacks Image: Lukasz Glowala/REUTERS Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine. In Romania , reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone. In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly , Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace." And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes." Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Romania would stand by Ukraine Image: Heather Khalifa/AP Photo/picture alliance Attacks on western Europe from the Mediterranean? Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy , France and Spain . The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet. There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible." French President Emmanuel Macron said the CIA had not warned France of possible drone attacks from international waters Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus. This article was originally published in German. https://www.artsjournal.com/uq/2026/10/a.text: Skip to main content Skip to primary sidebar This weekend’s online “ArtsFuse” carries an interview with me by Aaron Cohen (reproduced below) . I will be speaking about my recent novel “The Disciple” for the Wagner Society of New York on October 15 — information here . I will be speaking about Wagner, Seidl, and Chicago for the Wagner Society of America on October 27 — information here . The Disciple: A Wagnerian Tale of the Gilded Age resurrects Wagner’s American apostle—and a progressive, populist musical culture that New York has largely forgotten. In 1885, two years after Richard Wagner’s death, the Hungarian-born conductor Anton Seidl arrived in America. He would become New York’s most beloved conductor before fading into near-total obscurity by the mid-20 th century. Cultural historian Joseph Horowitz has spent decades recovering Seidl’s remarkable career from the archives. His new novel brings the man, the musician, and his vanished cultural world vividly to life. We spoke about the Gilded Age’s lost American canon—and how a historian came to write fiction. Arts Fuse: Anton Seidl is the central figure in your newest book , The Disciple: A Wagnerian Tale of the Gilded Age . So who was he? Joseph Horowitz: Anton Seidl was Wagner’s surrogate son , and he lived at Wahnfried. Wagner regarded him as the supreme interpreter of his music. It was Seidl who took Wagner’s Ring Cycle on tour in Europe and Russia, premiering it all over that part of the world. Wagner told him to get out of Wahnfried or he’d never grow up. He advised him to go to the New World. And Wagner predicted correctly that his operas would be more welcomed in America than in Europe and that he would be less controversial, which is exactly what happened. Seidl arrived in 1885 and became Wagner’s apostle in the New World. The more I read, the more I discovered that there was a halo around this man’s name. Every time you came across Anton Seidl, it was as if the heavens opened. You have Arthur Farwell in the 1940s remembering Anton Seidl in Musical Quarterly , and he says this was the greatest moment in the history of American classical music. Seidl wasn’t somebody like the celebrity conductors of today. He was not only esteemed but loved . AF: How did you come to rediscover him? Horowitz: I did it in the best possible way, which is digging into uncatalogued, undigitized archives. One was at Columbia University , called the Seidl Archive, and the other was the Seidl Society Archive at the Brooklyn Historical Society. What you had in the case of Seidl were two individuals who kept everything. One was his wife, then his widow. She kept everything. And then she gave it all to Columbia University, and everything is there. And the other was Laura Langford, whom we haven’t mentioned, who was the head of the Seidl Society. This is a woman who was a clairvoyant, a theosophist, a student of Madame Blavatsky in London, who became the major impresario in Brooklyn. Hello?! The major impresario in Brooklyn in the 1880s and 1890s was a woman, okay? They gave more concerts than the New York Philharmonic. That’s all due to Laura Langford , and she kept everything. Between these two women, there’s an immense repository of archival information that to this day has been very little explored except by me. AF: That would explain why , when I read your books, I feel like you are a time traveler. You could not possibly have heard these concerts in the 1880s and 1890s, and yet when I read your books, you’re living with these people and events. Horowitz: I somewhat live in the 1880s and 90s. It would not be a good time to be ill or to be poor. Other than that, it was a great time. Anyway, in Brooklyn Seidl conducted on Coney Island 14 times a week in the summertime. This is one of the things I discovered, something I had to absorb. I had to absorb many things. One day I’m rummaging through this stuff at the Brooklyn Historical Society, and I discover a piece of paper with handwriting in pencil. What is it? It’s a speech that Seidl had written to deliver somewhere in Brooklyn about the democratization of opera and music and how it’s more important that poor people hear this music than the rich people who chat in their boxes. We’re talking about a man who purchased a summer house in the Catskills, who became an American citizen, who spoke English (however imperfectly), who conducted concerts exclusively of American works, who threw open his door to the American composer. I was stunned. Had I not had the opportunity to actually finger Seidl’s letters and other memorabilia, I would never have acquired such a sense of intimacy. I could never have written a novel about him. That’s the cost of screens: they make everything vicarious. AF: Your books Moral Fire and Wagner Nights argue that American classical music peaked in the 1890s, during Seidl’s time here. Why was that? Horowitz: That’s when it’s most robust, most exciting, most influential nationally. And that’s when it’s healthiest because the focus was on the composer, on the prospect of creating an American canon. Not the great orchestras or the great violinists or the great pianists or the great conductors. But: how are we going to found an American compositional canon? And everybody assumed that by 2026 orchestras in this country would be mainly playing American music, which of course has not happened. AF: Other than Seidl, who are the historical personalities we should be paying attention to? Horowitz: There are a number of immense, colossal figures. Henry Higginson is one in Boston. Theodore Thomas is one. But in New York, it’s Antonín Dvořák and Anton Seidl. Of course, I was aware of Dvořák and his New World Symphony. I knew that he had taught at the National Conservatory of Music in New York, but I didn’t know the context. Jeannette Thurber, who ran the conservatory, offered free scholarships to all Black students. Why did she do that? It wasn’t only because she was a humanitarian ; it’s because she knew that the future music of the United States would be Black. Henry Krehbiel, the leading music critic of the time, knew that too, and he wrote the first book-length musical study of African American folk songs. Dvořák knew that instinctively. And the climate was amazingly progressive, humane, and farsighted. Anton Seidl in 1895. Photo: WikiMedia AF: Henry Krehbiel and Laura Langford are the major secondary characters in The Disciple . What drew you to them as characters? Horowitz: The whole saga – Anton Seidl, Laura Langford, Henry Krehbiel – is a gift to the novelist. You couldn’t make it up. Langford, who’s completely forgotten today, is a precursor to the New Woman. It’s revealing – of the times in which she lived – that she could only thrive in a contingent relationship to a man. Her husband ran the Brighton Beach Railroad. When he died and Seidl died, Langford drifted into obscurity. But she was a force : she drove her Seidl Society like a locomotive. Many men resented her as a bossy female in a man’s world. She grew up in the Civil War South, and her career as a journalist and impresario was partly an act of penance. The context, as with Wagnerism, was uplift . Her theosophy and clairvoyance were part of the same picture. Like Seidl, she was a moral force. And so was Krehbiel, for whom the moral criterion was paramount – that’s what “great music” was about. It may sound musty today, but it was fabulously empowering, this emphasis on human betterment. Langford brought African American orphans to Brighton Beach for turkey dinner and Wagner for dessert. Krehbiel was a tireless advocate for “African American folksongs.” His innumerable friendships included Harry Burleigh – Dvořák’s Black assistant, who was the pivotal figure in turning the sorrow songs into concert songs. Americans have no idea how potent the arts were in the late Gilded Age. They only think of robber barons and wealth snobs in their opera boxes. It’s not only a caricature – it’s a caricature that deprives us of an arts legacy we need to know. Americans were much more intensely engaged in the arts in the late nineteenth century than they are today. There’s really no comparison. The best-known image of Gilded Age opera is Gounod’s Faust at the Academy of Music, as evoked by Edith Wharton in The Age of Innocence as a showcase for the social elite. But the same Academy of Music housed an underground “beer cavern” where the hoi polloi congregated between acts, mingling with the artists. A lot of the chatter was in German or Italian. A few decades later, the Metropolitan Opera became a site of class warfare, with the Germanic Wagnerites shushing the boxholders. The boxholders rebelled in 1891 and threw the Germans out. But the Germans were strong and eventually came back. And yet there are social historians who insist that the museums and opera houses of the late Gilded Age manifested “class hegemony.” That’s an ideological hunch, not an empirical observation. It drives me crazy. AF: What was the music of the 1890s like? Horowitz: Well, first of all, you have the New World Symphony in 1893, an American work that was premiered by Seidl at Carnegie Hall. The American Suite by Dvořák and the Violin Sonatina are even more American. This is a guy who , for a period of three years , changed his tune and, like Kurt Weill, became an American composer. This is not an overstatement if you know the American Suite. The American Suite, unlike the New World Symphony, doesn’t even sound like “Dvořák . ” It’s a series of American postcards. So the American output in the 1890s includes three or four pieces by Antonín Dvořák. “Stars and Stripes Forever” was composed in the 1890s. “Maple Leaf Rag” was composed in the 1890s. Victor Herbert’s Second Cello Concerto, an excellent work, was composed in the 1890s and premiered under Anton Seidl. “Jubilee” by George Chadwick was composed in the 1890s and should be as well-known as “Stars and Stripes Forever.” But the kicker is that Charles Ives is already composing some of the greatest American concert songs as a student at Yale in the 1890s. After World War I , Aaron Copland and Virgil Thomson sold us a bill of goods – that no American music of consequence was composed before 1910. I call that the “standard narrative.” It’s still stifling. AF: You have been known primarily as a writer of nonfiction. When did you decide to write a novel about Seidl? Horowitz: The crucial moment was when I wrote a young people’s book about Dvořák in America as fiction. I’d never thought to write fiction, but I figured , if I’m writing this book for kids, it’ll be more entertaining, more accessible , if I do it with dialogue. So there is a chapter where I’ve got Seidl and Dvořák at Fleischmann’s Cafe. Every afternoon, Dvořák and Seidl would sit at the round table on the second floor of Fleischmann’s Cafe, and one would be drinking beers and the other smoking cigars. They spoke very little, but they met every day, and they were well-known public personalities. I created a scene in which they’re discussing the impending premiere of the New World Symphony. This was one of the spookiest things that ever happened to me as a scholar. I discovered I could hear Seidl talk, that I knew what he would say. That planted a seed. And eventually I wrote my novel. AF: The characters in The Disciple were real people, but most of the dialogue is your invention. Could we classify this book as historical fiction? Horowitz: In some respects, The Disciple would be more accurately called “creative nonfiction” than “historical fiction.” For the most part, I did not create the events in the book – I elaborated events that we know took place. In any event, the distinction between “fiction” and “nonfiction” deserves to be scrutinized. My “nonfiction” account of Seidl in New York is Wagner Nights: An American History , which was published in 1994. But a book of that kind, if decently done, requires lots of imagination; it’s not just an assemblage of facts culled from the historical record. For instance, there’s a scene in Wagner Nights in which I imagine what’s in Laura Langford’s head when she speaks at a Brighton Beach “Wagner Night.” In fact, I believe I have discovered, at least for myself, that “historical fiction” is an invaluable tool for the historian – you learn new things when you add dialogue ; it brings the story to life. AF: In 2023 , you published The Marriage: The Mahlers in New York , which focused on Gustav and Alma Mahler’s time here. This is the same world of classical music in New York as The Disciple , although ten years later. So The Disciple is a prequel to The Marriage ? Horowitz: The Disciple was written long ago. It’s only been published recently. But I wrote The Disciple and then I decided I should write a second novel as a sequel about Mahler in New York because Mahler in New York can only be understood in the context of Seidl in New York. Then I decided they were one big book. Then my friend Antonio Muñoz Molina, the famous Spanish novelist, read both novels and he said, no, these are two books. And I thought I better publish the Mahler one first because nobody’s heard of Seidl. And that’s why only now is the book The Disciple: A Wagnerian Tale of the Gilded Age being published, written so long ago that I actually cannot even recall the act of writing it. And I read it and marvel that I ever managed to write it. AF: Seidl died suddenly in 1898. What was lost? Horowitz: Seidl was bigger than Toscanini, bigger than Bernstein. Wagnerism is the dominant theme of American cultural and intellectual life for a period of about 20 years. If you read The Atlantic Monthly , you’re reading articles about Wagner. One thing that’s immensely important is that , if Seidl had not died at the age of 47 in the 1890s, he would have established a Wagner festival in Brooklyn, commensurate in importance and prestige with Bayreuth. This horrible tarnishing of Wagner’s legacy by swastikas at Bayreuth, there would have been an alternative to that. So the influence of Wagner via Seidl was immense. And Seidl himself is an indescribably charismatic personality. It was my good fortune to discover, or rediscover, Anton Seidl. AF: A final word? Horowitz: I wrote The Disciple partly as an exhortation to fundamentally rethink the Gilded Age. It’s not just a book for Wagnerites or music lovers. Aaron Cohen is an award-winning radio producer and Director of Broadcast Operations at New York Public Radio. His classical-music features have been heard on WNYC, WQXR, American Public Media, the WFMT Radio Network, and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
